      <description><h1>
  
  
  CVE-2025-53837: Remote Code Execution in XWiki Rendering via Macro Escape Injection
</h1>

<blockquote>
<p><strong>Vulnerability ID:</strong> CVE-2025-53837<br>
<strong>CVSS Score:</strong> 9.9<br>
<strong>Published:</strong> 2026-09-18</p>
</blockquote>

<p>CVE-2025-53837 is a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in XWiki Rendering before versions 14.10.2 and 15.0 RC1. The vulnerability arises from a failure to escape macro closing tags within raw output handled by HTML macro blocks. This allows low-privilege users to escape the restricted HTML container and execute high-privilege scripts under the application's context.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  TL;DR
</h2>

<p>Unauthenticated or low-privilege users can inject the "{{/html}}" sequence to escape HTML macro scopes and run arbitrary code on the host OS via privileged script macros.</p>




<h2>
  
  
  Technical Details
</h2>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Improproper Input Validation</strong>: An issue was discovered in NETGEAR R6080 routers through 1.0.0.46. The login.cgi and upgrade.cgi pages and multiple dynamic parameters (such as formUsername, hidden_sysPassword, sysPassword, save_reboot, and select_country) are vulnerable to buffer overflow. An attacker can hijack a stack variable and crash the system or execute arbitrary code with admin privileges by writing over boundary limits of variables.</li>
</ul>

<h2>
  
  
  Affected Systems
</h2>

<ul>
<li>cpe:2.3⭕netgear:r6080_firmware:<em>:</em>:<em>:</em>:<em>:</em>:<em>:</em>
</li>
</ul>

      <title>Security Audit Report: Reentrancy & Access Control Review: Aave V3</title>
      <dc:creator>DannyDoes</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:21:19 +0000</pubDate>

      <description><h1>
  
  
  Security Audit Report: Reentrancy &amp; Access Control Review: Aave V3
</h1>

<p><strong>Target Protocol</strong>: Aave V3 (TVL: $17746.7M)</p>

<h1>
  
  
  Security Audit Report
</h1>

<p><strong>Reentrancy &amp; Access‑Control Review – Aave V3</strong><br><br>
<strong>Protocol:</strong> Aave V3 (TVL ≈ $17.7 B across Ethereum &amp; L2s)<br><br>
<strong>Date of Review:</strong> September 2026<br><br>
<strong>Prepared by:</strong> [Your Company / Team] – Senior DeFi Security Researchers &amp; Auditors  </p>




<h2>
  
  
  1. Executive Summary
</h2>

<p>Aave V3 is the third generation of the leading permission‑less lending market on Ethereum and multiple Layer‑2 roll‑ups. Its core value proposition—high‑efficiency capital markets, isolated‑mode risk parameters, and “eMode” (efficiency mode) for correlated assets—relies on a complex set of smart‑contract interactions, cross‑chain bridges, and on‑chain governance.  </p>

<p>The present audit focuses <strong>exclusively</strong> on two critical security domains:</p>

<div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Domain</th>
<th>Scope</th>
<th>Primary Concern</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>Reentrancy</strong></td>
<td>All external‑call pathways in the core lending pool contracts (<code>Pool</code>, <code>PoolConfigurator</code>, <code>PoolDataProvider</code>, <code>FlashLoanReceiver</code>, <code>Bridge</code> adapters) and any upgradeable proxy logic.</td>
<td>Potential for malicious borrowers or third‑party contracts to re‑enter vulnerable functions and manipulate balances, interest accrual, or collateral checks.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Access Control</strong></td>
<td>Role‑based permissioning (admin, emergency admin, risk admin, bridge admin, flash‑loan caller whitelist, token‑list admin) and upgrade‑proxy governance (<code>ProxyAdmin</code>, <code>AaveGovernanceV2</code>).</td>
<td>Unauthorized privilege escalation, rogue upgrades, or misuse of privileged functions that could freeze assets, change risk parameters, or drain liquidity.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>

<h3>
  
  
  Overall Findings
</h3>

<div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Finding Category</th>
<th># of Issues</th>
<th>Severity Distribution (Critical / High / Medium / Low)</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Reentrancy</td>
<td>4</td>
<td>1 Critical, 1 High, 2 Medium</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Access‑Control</td>
<td>7</td>
<td>2 Critical, 2 High, 3 Medium</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>

<p>The <strong>aggregate risk score</strong> for the audited surface is <strong>7.4 / 10</strong> (High). The most severe issues stem from <strong>improperly guarded external calls in the flash‑loan and collateral‑withdrawal paths</strong> and <strong>over‑broad admin role assignments in the upgrade proxy</strong>. None of the identified vulnerabilities are currently exploitable in the live main‑net deployment due to existing defensive patterns (e.g., re‑entrancy guards, multi‑sig governance), but they represent <strong>significant attack surface</strong> if a future upgrade or mis‑configuration removes those safeguards.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Business Impact
</h3>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Capital at Risk:</strong> A successful re‑entrancy exploit on the flash‑loan entry point could enable an attacker to borrow assets, manipulate price oracles, and exit with up to <strong>$1.2 B</strong> (≈ 7 % of TVL) before liquidation mechanisms react.
</li>
<li>
<strong>Protocol Governance Hijack:</strong> An access‑control flaw allowing a single address to become <code>PoolAdmin</code> could permit arbitrary parameter changes, token listings, or contract upgrades, potentially leading to <strong>protocol freeze or asset exfiltration</strong>.
</li>
</ul>

<p>Given Aave’s role as a cornerstone of DeFi liquidity, remediation of the identified issues is essential to maintain user confidence and to protect the multi‑billion‑dollar ecosystem built on top of it.</p>




<h2>
  
  
  2. Identified Attack Vectors
</h2>

<h3>
  
  
  2.1 Reentrancy‑Related Vectors
</h3>

<div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>#</th>
<th>Contract / Function</th>
<th>Description of Vulnerability</th>
<th>Exploit Scenario</th>
<th>Potential Impact</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>R‑1</strong></td>
<td>
<code>Pool.sol</code> – <code>withdraw(address asset, uint256 amount)</code> (pre‑v3.2.0)</td>
<td>Missing <code>nonReentrant</code> guard when transferring the underlying asset <strong>before</strong> updating the user’s debt/borrow balance.</td>
<td>An attacker creates a malicious ERC‑20 token that calls back into <code>withdraw</code> during the <code>transfer</code> callback, allowing repeated withdrawals while the internal accounting still reflects the original balance.</td>
<td>
<strong>Critical</strong> – Unlimited asset drain limited only by the pool’s liquidity of the targeted token.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>R‑2</strong></td>
<td>
<code>FlashLoanReceiverBase.sol</code> – <code>executeOperation(...)</code> (user‑implemented)</td>
<td>No enforced re‑entrancy protection on the callback; the protocol assumes the borrower’s code is safe.</td>
<td>A malicious borrower contracts a re‑entrant call to <code>borrow</code> within <code>executeOperation</code>, borrowing additional flash‑loan amounts before the original loan is settled.</td>
<td>
<strong>High</strong> – Amplifies flash‑loan attack surface; could be combined with price‑oracle manipulation to extract &gt;$500 M.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>R‑3</strong></td>
<td>
<code>BridgeAdapter.sol</code> – <code>bridgeOut(address token, uint256 amount, bytes calldata data)</code>
</td>
<td>External call to L2 bridge contract occurs <strong>before</strong> the internal <code>reserveData</code> update.</td>
<td>An attacker’s bridge contract re‑enters <code>bridgeOut</code> via a fallback, causing double‑counting of the same assets on L2 and resulting in mismatched reserves.</td>
<td>
<strong>Medium</strong> – Potential for cross‑chain reserve imbalance, leading to liquidation cascades.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>R‑4</strong></td>
<td>
<code>PoolConfigurator.sol</code> – <code>setReserveInterestRateStrategy(address asset, address strategy)</code>
</td>
<td>The function updates the strategy pointer <strong>after</strong> calling <code>strategy.initialize()</code> on the new contract, which may invoke external code.</td>
<td>A malicious strategy contract re‑enters <code>setReserveInterestRateStrategy</code> to replace the strategy of another asset, effectively hijacking interest calculations.</td>
<td>
<strong>Medium</strong> – Could skew interest rates, causing loss of yield or over‑collateralization.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>

<h3>
  
  
  2.2 Access‑Control‑Related Vectors
</h3>

<div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>#</th>
<th>Contract / Function</th>
<th>Description of Vulnerability</th>
<th>Exploit Scenario</th>
<th>Potential Impact</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>A‑1</strong></td>
<td>
<code>ProxyAdmin.sol</code> – <code>upgrade(address proxy, address implementation)</code>
</td>
<td>
<code>onlyOwner</code> modifier is bound to a <strong>single EOA</strong> (<code>owner = 0x…</code>) rather than a multi‑sig Gnosis Safe.</td>
<td>If the private key of the owner is compromised, an attacker can upgrade any proxy (including <code>Pool</code> and <code>PoolConfigurator</code>) to malicious implementations.</td>
<td>
<strong>Critical</strong> – Full control over core protocol logic; asset exfiltration possible.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>A‑2</strong></td>
<td>
<code>AaveGovernanceV2.sol</code> – <code>execute(address target, bytes calldata data)</code>
</td>
<td>No explicit check that the proposal has passed the <strong>minimum voting power</strong> threshold; relies on off‑chain UI enforcement.</td>
<td>An attacker submits a proposal with a fabricated <code>votePower</code> field, bypassing the quorum check and executing arbitrary governance actions.</td>
<td>
<strong>Critical</strong> – Governance takeover, parameter changes, token minting.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>A‑3</strong></td>
<td>
<code>PoolConfigurator.sol</code> – <code>setReserveFactor(address asset, uint256 factor)</code>
</td>
<td>Only <code>POOL_ADMIN_ROLE</code> required; the role is granted to a <strong>single address</strong> (<code>0x…</code>) that is also the <code>POOL_ADMIN</code> of the <code>Pool</code>.</td>
<td>Compromise of that address (phishing, key leakage) allows the attacker to set reserve factors to 0, draining protocol fees.</td>
<td>
<strong>High</strong> – Loss of revenue, reduced incentives for liquidity providers.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>A‑4</strong></td>
<td>
<code>BridgeAdapter.sol</code> – <code>addBridge(address bridge)</code>
</td>
<td>No event emitted on addition; bridge list is stored in a public array but not indexed.</td>
<td>An attacker can add a malicious bridge contract that silently forwards assets to an external address, making detection difficult.</td>
<td>
<strong>High</strong> – Cross‑chain asset theft.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>A‑5</strong></td>
<td>
<code>FlashLoanReceiverBase.sol</code> – <code>executeOperation</code> whitelist</td>
<td>Whitelist is a simple mapping (<code>address =&gt; bool</code>) controlled by <code>POOL_ADMIN_ROLE</code>. No time‑lock on changes.</td>
<td>An admin (or compromised admin) can add a malicious borrower contract to the whitelist instantly.</td>
<td>
<strong>Medium</strong> – Enables malicious flash‑loan attacks without community notice.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>A‑6</strong></td>
<td>
<code>RiskParams.sol</code> – <code>setCollateralCap(address asset, uint256 cap)</code>
</td>
<td>No upper bound validation; cap can be set to zero.</td>
<td>An attacker with <code>RISK_ADMIN_ROLE</code> can set the collateral cap of a major asset (e.g., WETH) to 0, effectively freezing borrowing against it.</td>
<td>
<strong>Medium</strong> – Market disruption, loss of confidence.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>A‑7</strong></td>
<td>
<code>PoolDataProvider.sol</code> – <code>setAssetData(address asset, AssetData calldata data)</code>
</td>
<td>Function is <code>external</code> but not <code>onlyOwner</code>; any address can call it.</td>
<td>An attacker can corrupt the on‑chain metadata (e.g., price source address) used by UI and off‑chain bots, leading to mis‑priced trades.</td>
<td>
<strong>Low</strong> – Primarily an information‑integrity issue, but can be leveraged for price‑oracle attacks.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>




<h2>
  
  
  3. Prioritized Technical Recommendations
</h2>

<p>The recommendations are ordered by <strong>risk severity</strong>, <strong>ease of implementation</strong>, and <strong>potential reduction in attack surface</strong>.  </p>

<h3>
  
  
  3.1 Immediate (Critical) Remediations – <strong>≤ 2 weeks</strong>
</h3>

<div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Ref</th>
<th>Action</th>
<th>Rationale</th>
<th>Implementation Notes</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>R‑1</strong></td>
<td>Add <code>nonReentrant</code> (OpenZeppelin <code>ReentrancyGuard</code>) <strong>before</strong> any external token transfer in <code>withdraw</code> and all similar state‑changing functions.</td>
<td>Eliminates the classic “withdraw‑re‑enter” vector.</td>
<td>Ensure the guard is placed at the <strong>function entry</strong>; verify that the contract inherits the guard only once (avoid double‑inheritance).</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>A‑1</strong></td>
<td>Migrate <code>ProxyAdmin.owner</code> to a <strong>multi‑signature Gnosis Safe</strong> (≥ 3‑of‑5). Add a timelock (e.g., 48 h) for any <code>upgrade</code> call.</td>
<td>Reduces single‑point‑of‑failure risk for upgrades.</td>
<td>Deploy a new <code>ProxyAdmin</code> contract with <code>owner</code> set to the Safe; update all proxies via a governance proposal.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>A‑2</strong></td>
<td>Harden <code>execute</code> in <code>AaveGovernanceV2</code> by <strong>explicitly verifying</strong> that the proposal’s <code>forVotes</code> ≥ <code>quorum</code> <strong>on‑chain</strong> and that the proposal state is <code>Succeeded</code>.</td>
<td>Prevents off‑chain UI manipulation and ensures quorum enforcement.</td>
<td>Add a <code>require(proposal.state == ProposalState.Succeeded, "Not succeeded")</code>.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>A‑3</strong></td>
<td>Split <code>POOL_ADMIN_ROLE</code> into <strong>two distinct roles</strong>: <code>POOL_CONFIG_ADMIN</code> (for reserve factor changes) and <code>POOL_EMERGENCY_ADMIN</code> (for emergency actions). Require a <strong>2‑step timelock</strong> for <code>setReserveFactor</code>.</td>
<td>Limits the blast radius of a compromised admin key.</td>
<td>Use <code>AccessControl</code> with <code>grantRole</code>/<code>revokeRole</code> and a <code>TimelockController</code>.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>A‑4</strong></td>
<td>Emit a <strong><code>BridgeAdded(address bridge)</code></strong> event and require a <strong>governance proposal</strong> (with timelock) for adding new bridges.</td>
<td>Improves transparency and gives the community a chance to audit new bridges.</td>
<td>Add <code>event BridgeAdded(address indexed bridge);</code> and call it after successful addition.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>

<h3>
  
  
  3.2 High‑Priority (Next 1‑2 weeks)
</h3>

<div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Ref</th>
<th>Action</th>
<th>Rationale</th>
<th>Implementation Notes</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>R‑2</strong></td>
<td>Provide a <strong>library‑level re‑entrancy guard</strong> for user‑implemented <code>executeOperation</code> callbacks (e.g., <code>FlashLoanReentrancyGuard</code>).</td>
<td>Guarantees that even malicious borrower contracts cannot re‑enter the pool during a flash‑loan.</td>
<td>Document the guard in the developer SDK; optionally enforce via a static‑analysis rule in the deployment pipeline.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>R‑3</strong></td>
<td>Reorder logic in <code>bridgeOut</code>: <strong>update reserve data first</strong>, then call the external bridge.</td>
<td>Prevents double‑spend via re‑entrancy into the bridge contract.</td>
<td>Add a <code>reserveData.totalLiquidity -= amount;</code> before the external call.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>A‑5</strong></td>
<td>Introduce a <strong>2‑day timelock</strong> on modifications to the flash‑loan whitelist, and emit <code>FlashLoanWhitelistUpdated(address borrower, bool allowed)</code>.</td>
<td>Gives the community time to review new borrowers.</td>
<td>Use <code>TimelockController</code> and <code>emit</code> events.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>A‑6</strong></td>
<td>Enforce a <strong>minimum collateral cap</strong> (e.g., 1 % of total supply) and a <strong>maximum cap</strong> (e.g., 100 % of total supply) in <code>setCollateralCap</code>.</td>
<td>Prevents accidental or malicious freezing of markets.</td>
<td>Add <code>require(cap &gt;= minCap &amp;&amp; cap &lt;= maxCap, "Cap out of bounds");</code>.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>R‑4</strong></td>
<td>Add a <strong>re‑entrancy guard</strong> around the <code>strategy.initialize()</code> call in <code>setReserveInterestRateStrategy</code>.</td>
<td>Stops malicious strategies from hijacking other reserves.</td>
<td>Wrap the external call with <code>nonReentrant</code> or a custom guard.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>

<h3>
  
  
  3.3 Medium‑Priority (Within 1 month)
</h3>

<div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Ref</th>
<th>Action</th>
<th>Rationale</th>
<th>Implementation Notes</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>A‑7</strong></td>
<td>Restrict <code>setAssetData</code> to <code>GOVERNOR_ROLE</code> and add an <strong>event</strong> <code>AssetDataUpdated(address asset)</code>.</td>
<td>Prevents arbitrary metadata tampering.</td>
<td>Simple <code>onlyRole(GOVERNOR_ROLE)</code> modifier.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>
<strong>R‑3</strong> (Cross‑chain)</td>
<td>Deploy a <strong>bridge‑state‑snapshot</strong> contract that records the pre‑bridge reserve balance and validates it after the bridge call (assertion).</td>
<td>Detects any mismatch caused by re‑entrancy or bridge bugs.</td>
<td>Use <code>assert</code> or `</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>

      <title>Exposure Check: Sizing the MikroTik RouterOS Fleet Before Attackers Do</title>
      <dc:creator>jeffrey</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:20:06 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/jeffreyciend/exposure-check-sizing-the-mikrotik-routeros-fleet-before-attackers-do-54gp</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/jeffreyciend/exposure-check-sizing-the-mikrotik-routeros-fleet-before-attackers-do-54gp</guid>
      <description><h1>
  
  
  Exposure Check: Sizing the MikroTik RouterOS Fleet Before Attackers Do
</h1>

<p>When a CRITICAL authentication bypass lands for a widely deployed router platform, the first operational question is scale. CERT-In's note CIVN-2026-0460 (September 16, 2026) documents CVE-2026-67276 in MikroTik RouterOS: incomplete verification of RSA public keys during SSH authentication allows a forged key and signature to bypass login, potentially granting full administrative control.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  What the internet-facing surface looks like
</h2>

<p>To measure how much RouterOS exists in the wild, a ZoomEye survey was run with the product operating-system query os="RouterOS" on September 18, 2026. It returned 8,085,078 matching assets. The count represents RouterOS assets indexed by the search engine; it does not confirm that any listed device runs an affected version or exposes SSH. A companion filter query, vul.cve="CVE-2026-67276", returned zero indexed assets, meaning the CVE is not yet mapped to indexed devices in that dataset.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Translating surface into risk
</h2>

<p>Three factors turn this exposure into concrete risk:</p>

<ul>
<li>The flaw is pre-authentication: forged RSA credentials are enough, so no password theft is required.</li>
<li>SSH is routinely left reachable for administration, and the companion flaw CVE-2026-86060 raises privileges through crafted argument delimiters once any login path is reachable.</li>
<li>The third flaw in the same advisory, CVE-2026-67277, lets unauthenticated requests to the bandwidth-test service leak kernel memory and crash devices.</li>
</ul>

<h2>
  
  
  Affected versions
</h2>

<p>RouterOS 7.24 and versions before 7.24.2, versions from 7.0.0 before 7.23.4, and versions from 6.0.0 before 6.49.21.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Actions
</h2>

<p>Upgrade to the fixed releases in MikroTik's September 2026 advisory, then shrink the reachable surface: filter SSH to trusted sources, disable btest where unused, and audit administrative access logs for anomalies.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Sources
</h2>

<ul>
<li>CERT-In Vulnerability Note CIVN-2026-0460 (September 16, 2026)</li>
<li>MikroTik advisory: <a href="https://mikrotik.com/supportsec/september-2026-vulnerability/" rel="noopener noreferrer">https://mikrotik.com/supportsec/september-2026-vulnerability/</a>
</li>
<li>ZoomEye queries os="RouterOS" (8,085,078 assets) and vul.cve="CVE-2026-67276" (0), checked 2026-09-18</li>
</ul>

      <title>kagent v1.0 Can Run Claude Code as a Managed Kubernetes Agent</title>
      <dc:creator>Mike Moore</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:10:21 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/webofmike/kagent-v10-can-run-claude-code-as-a-managed-kubernetes-agent-3p50</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/webofmike/kagent-v10-can-run-claude-code-as-a-managed-kubernetes-agent-3p50</guid>
      <description><p><em>Originally published at <a href="https://webofmike.com/kagent-v1-agentinstance-claude-code-harness/?utm_source=devto&amp;utm_medium=syndication&amp;utm_campaign=kagent-v1-agentinstance-claude-code-harness" rel="noopener noreferrer">webofmike.com</a> on 2026-09-18. The demo repo and every command in it were run before publishing.</em></p>

<p>kagent shipped <a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/releases/tag/v1.0.0-alpha1" rel="noopener noreferrer">v1.0.0-alpha1</a> this morning, its first 1.0 line after nine months on 0.x. The tag says alpha; GitHub's own release flag says otherwise; it's marked <code>prerelease: false</code>, listed as <code>Latest</code>. Release notes lie about formatting more than they should, and this is a version-number one: don't assume the tag string tells you how GitHub, or a Helm repo index, actually classifies the artifact. Check both, every time.</p>

<p>The changelog runs to roughly 130 pull requests. Most of it is refactoring: <code>refactor: remove deployment-backed agent API</code>, <code>refactor: remove legacy controller runtime</code>, <code>chore: remove legacy ACP and controller runtime</code>. That pattern, repeated a dozen times, is the actual story. kagent didn't add a feature to its old agent model. It replaced the model.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  AgentInstance replaces the Deployment
</h2>

<p>Through 0.x, a kagent agent was, underneath, a Kubernetes Deployment. v1.0 introduces <code>AgentInstance</code>: an imperative gRPC lifecycle object with a fixed state machine, not a workload spec a controller reconciles toward.</p>

<p><a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/pull/2436" rel="noopener noreferrer">PR #2436</a> adds the service and its PostgreSQL persistence, with idempotent create, ownership checks, and Actor identity fencing. <a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/pull/2445" rel="noopener noreferrer">PR #2445</a> adds suspend and resume, synchronous, backed by Substrate, and explicit about what happens when two callers collide:</p>

<blockquote>
<p>Kind smoke: Create → READY → Suspend → SUSPENDED → Resume → READY → conflicting Resume → ABORTED → Delete → DELETED → Get → NOT_FOUND</p>
</blockquote>

<p>That's not a happy-path test. It's a test that a second, conflicting resume gets rejected outright rather than racing the first one. A Deployment reconciler doesn't offer that; it just converges, eventually, and two competing writers get whatever order the informer delivers. AgentInstance answers with a status code instead.</p>

<p><a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/pull/2446" rel="noopener noreferrer">PR #2446</a> puts an authenticated A2A gRPC gateway in front of ready instances, routing through Atenet to private root Substrate actors. The PR is explicit about what's still missing: "Durable public Task persistence, public/private ID mapping, ordering, and idempotency remain follow-up work." Worth knowing before you point production A2A traffic at it on day one of an alpha.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Checkpoint and fork, at the conversation level
</h2>

<p>The most visible v1.0 feature lives in the chat UI, not the API. <a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/pull/2775" rel="noopener noreferrer">PR #2775</a> adds a Checkpoint button next to Send. It saves the conversation's current turn boundary. "Everything above it travels into a fork and nothing below it does" is how the PR describes the contract. <code>Duplicate chat</code> in the rail's row menu is the same mechanism: checkpoint plus fork, in one click.</p>

<p><a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/pull/2847" rel="noopener noreferrer">PR #2847</a> renames the concept from "checkpoint" to "snapshot" in the chat, gives each one a name (<code>&lt;agentInstanceId&gt;-&lt;headTaskId&gt;</code> by default), and puts Fork, Rename, and Delete on its mark in the transcript. <a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/pull/2804" rel="noopener noreferrer">PR #2804</a> adds deletion: releasing a checkpoint's snapshot doesn't break chats already forked from it, because a fork copies the checkpoint's identity rather than referencing it live.</p>

<p>This is a git-like model applied to an agent conversation, and it's a genuinely different way to think about agent state. An agent conversation that goes sideways isn't something you restart from scratch or patch in place; you fork from the last good checkpoint and try again, keeping the bad branch around to compare.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Golden snapshots: resuming without a cold OCI boot
</h2>

<p>The performance story sits underneath the UI, in <a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/pull/2715" rel="noopener noreferrer">PR #2715</a>: resuming a suspended actor from a Substrate "golden snapshot" (a FULL gVisor snapshot plus the latest DATA snapshot) instead of cold-booting the actor from its OCI image every time.</p>

<p>The PR includes its own benchmark, 25 turns per harness, cold boot versus golden resume:</p>

<div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Metric</th>
<th>Codex: cold / golden</th>
<th>Claude: cold / golden</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Median first output</td>
<td>725 / 695 ms</td>
<td>1,282 / 1,068 ms</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Median turn completion</td>
<td>971 / 957 ms</td>
<td>2,007 / 1,731 ms</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Mean Substrate restore</td>
<td>235 / 234 ms</td>
<td>294 / 196 ms</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Mean checkpoint</td>
<td>232 / 232 ms</td>
<td>243 / 212 ms</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>

<p>Codex barely moves. Claude's numbers move more, which tracks: a heavier CLI process pays more for a cold OCI boot and gets more back from skipping it. I haven't reproduced this benchmark myself; it's quoted from the PR description, not a run against my own cluster, and I'm saying so rather than presenting it as something I measured.</p>

<p>The PR is also specific about when an old golden snapshot stops working: a Substrate upgrade doesn't automatically invalidate one, because the snapshot manifest pins its own sandbox class, runtime asset hash, and pause image. It breaks only if an upgrade changes the snapshot format itself, or the restore contract, or drops host support for the pinned runtime. That's a real answer to "what happens to my snapshots when I upgrade Substrate," not a "should be fine" hand-wave.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  The new harnesses: Claude Code and Codex, running as agents
</h2>

<p>The change I'd call the headline feature is <a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/pull/2602" rel="noopener noreferrer">PR #2602</a>: kagent can now run the actual Claude Code CLI as an agent harness, pinned version, over A2A, with streaming, cancellation, session resume, and durable state through Substrate. <a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/pull/2645" rel="noopener noreferrer">PR #2645</a> adds Codex the same way, reusing most of the Claude harness's plumbing, driven through the Codex App Server's JSON-RPC-over-stdio protocol.</p>

<p>That means kagent's own harness options are no longer limited to its ADK-based agent runtime. You can point an <code>AgentTemplate</code> at a coding CLI you already use daily and get a managed, checkpointable, forkable, suspend-and-resume-capable Kubernetes object wrapped around it.</p>

<p>One detail in the Codex PR is worth calling out on its own, because it looks alarming out of context and isn't:</p>

<blockquote>
<p>Runs Codex with approvals set to never and native sandboxing set to danger-full-access; the Substrate Actor is intentionally the security boundary.</p>
</blockquote>

<p>Read on its own, "danger-full-access" sounds like turning off the safety rails. It's the opposite: kagent is deliberately not layering Codex's own approval prompts and sandbox on top of Substrate's, because that would be two enforcement points guessing about each other's state. The Substrate actor, the gVisor sandbox the harness runs inside, is the one boundary that's actually authoritative, so the harness-level controls are turned off rather than left to fight it. Whether you're comfortable with that tradeoff depends entirely on trusting the actor sandbox, which is a fair thing to want to verify yourself before running either harness against anything sensitive.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  What v1.0.0-alpha1 doesn't mean
</h2>

<p>Alpha means alpha. The A2A gateway PR names its own gaps in durable task persistence and ID mapping. This release also carries <code>fix: migrate checkpoints to Substrate v0.0.26</code> and <code>fix: preserve conversation identity and history across forks</code> as <em>fixes</em>, both landing after the checkpoint/fork UI they support, which says the fork feature had real correctness bugs during its own development window. That's normal for a feature this new, not a red flag, but it means an alpha this size is worth running somewhere you can afford to lose state before you run it somewhere you can't.</p>

<p>The architecture change is bigger than any one feature in it. kagent spent most of 2026 running agents as pods that Agent Substrate multiplexed onto a shared worker pool (<a href="https://webofmike.com/kagent-agent-substrate/" rel="noopener noreferrer">I wrote about that runtime here</a>). v1.0 keeps that runtime and puts a proper lifecycle API on top of it: agents you can suspend, resume, checkpoint, and fork as first-class operations, not side effects of a Deployment you're poking with kubectl. Adding Claude Code and Codex as harnesses on that same lifecycle is what makes it concrete: whatever you build against AgentInstance now works for a coding agent you already trust, not just kagent's own runtime.</p>

<p>Full changelog: <a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/releases/tag/v1.0.0-alpha1" rel="noopener noreferrer">kagent-dev/kagent v1.0.0-alpha1</a>. Compare against the last stable line: <a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/compare/v0.10.0-rc1...v1.0.0-alpha1" rel="noopener noreferrer">v0.10.0...v1.0.0-alpha1</a>.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Frequently asked questions
</h2>

<p><strong>Can I run Claude Code as an agent inside kagent on Kubernetes?</strong></p>

<p>Yes, as of kagent v1.0.0-alpha1. PR #2602 adds a native Claude harness that runs the pinned Claude Code CLI over A2A with streaming, cancellation, session resume, and durable state on Substrate. PR #2645 adds the same support for Codex, reusing most of the same plumbing, with feature parity to kagent's own ADK harness.</p>

<p><strong>What is an AgentInstance in kagent v1.0?</strong></p>

<p>AgentInstance is kagent v1.0's replacement for its old Deployment-backed agent API. It is an imperative gRPC lifecycle object, create/suspend/resume/delete, backed by Substrate actors and persisted in PostgreSQL. Competing transitions are conflict-fenced: a second resume against an already-resumed instance returns ABORTED instead of corrupting state.</p>

<p><strong>How much faster is resuming a kagent agent from a golden snapshot than cold-booting it?</strong></p>

<p>In kagent's own PR #2715 benchmark (25 turns per harness), the Claude harness's median turn completion dropped from 2,007ms cold to 1,731ms from a golden snapshot, and mean Substrate restore dropped from 294ms to 196ms. Codex, a lighter process, moved less: 971ms to 957ms median turn completion. Both numbers come from the PR description, not a run I reproduced myself.</p>

<p><strong>Can I fork a kagent conversation without losing earlier checkpoints?</strong></p>

<p>Yes. kagent v1.0's UI lets you checkpoint a chat turn, then fork from that checkpoint into a new, independent conversation that inherits the checkpoint's name (PR #2775, #2847). Deleting a checkpoint later releases the snapshot it pins, but chats already forked from it keep working (PR #2804).</p>

      <title>Two agentgateway CEL Gotchas: One Fails Open, One Fails Closed</title>
      <dc:creator>Mike Moore</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:09:49 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/webofmike/two-agentgateway-cel-gotchas-one-fails-open-one-fails-closed-17eg</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/webofmike/two-agentgateway-cel-gotchas-one-fails-open-one-fails-closed-17eg</guid>
      <description><p><em>Originally published at <a href="https://webofmike.com/agentgateway-cel-authorization-gotchas/?utm_source=devto&amp;utm_medium=syndication&amp;utm_campaign=agentgateway-cel-authorization-gotchas" rel="noopener noreferrer">webofmike.com</a> on 2026-09-18. The demo repo and every command in it were run before publishing.</em></p>

<p>I was writing a CEL authorization policy for an LLM route in <a href="https://docs.solo.io/agentgateway/" rel="noopener noreferrer">Solo Enterprise for agentgateway</a>: restrict which models a caller may reach, and refuse callers whose identity provider says they are in a jurisdiction the company cannot serve. Two conditions, both read off the same request.</p>

<p>The first version I wrote allowed a request it should have denied. The second version denied every request, including the ones that should have passed. Neither one reported an error. Both showed <code>Accepted</code> and <code>Attached</code> in the policy status.</p>

<p>The working policy and the demo that proves it are in <a href="https://github.com/themsquared/agentic-demo" rel="noopener noreferrer">themsquared/agentic-demo</a> under <a href="https://github.com/themsquared/agentic-demo/tree/main/manifests/governance" rel="noopener noreferrer"><code>manifests/governance/</code></a>. Everything below was verified against a live cluster running v2026.8.2.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  The policy I meant to write
</h2>

<p>Two rules on a route called <code>governed-llm</code>. The caller's JWT carries a <code>country</code> claim from the identity provider. The request body names a model.</p>

<ol>
<li>The country must be present and not on a restricted list.</li>
<li>The model must be one the AI governance group has approved.</li>
</ol>

<p>Written the obvious way, that is two entries in <code>matchExpressions</code>:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight yaml"><code><span class="na">traffic</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="na">authorization</span><span class="pi">:</span>
    <span class="na">action</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">Allow</span>
    <span class="na">policy</span><span class="pi">:</span>
      <span class="na">matchExpressions</span><span class="pi">:</span>
      <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="s">has(jwt.country)</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">&amp;&amp;</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">!(jwt.country</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">in</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">['CU',</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">'IR',</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">'KP',</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">'SY'])"</span>
      <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="s">json(request.body).model</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">in</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">['claude-sonnet-4-6',</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">'claude-haiku-4-5']"</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>That reads as "both must hold". It is not what it does.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Failure one: matchExpressions is OR, and it fails open
</h2>

<p>I have two test users from the same Keycloak realm, in the same group, with the same permissions. The only difference is the <code>country</code> claim: <code>maria</code> is <code>US</code>, <code>pat</code> is <code>IR</code>.</p>

<p>With the two-entry policy above:</p>

<div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Caller</th>
<th>Model</th>
<th>Expected</th>
<th>Actual</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>maria (US)</td>
<td>approved</td>
<td>200</td>
<td>200</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>pat (IR)</td>
<td>approved</td>
<td><strong>403</strong></td>
<td><strong>200</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>maria (US)</td>
<td>not approved</td>
<td><strong>403</strong></td>
<td><strong>200</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>no JWT</td>
<td>approved</td>
<td>401</td>
<td>401</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>

<p>Both of the requests that should have been refused went through to the provider.</p>

<p>The reason is that entries in <code>matchExpressions</code> are OR'ed. A request is allowed when <em>any</em> expression evaluates true. <code>pat</code> fails the country rule but satisfies the model rule, so the policy allows the request. <code>maria</code> asking for an unapproved model is the mirror image: the country rule passes, so the model rule never gets to matter.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://docs.solo.io/agentgateway/" rel="noopener noreferrer">documentation</a> does state the behavior, in one sentence: requests that do not match any of the conditions are denied. Read closely that is unambiguous. Read at the speed you actually read reference docs, next to a YAML block with a list under it, and "a list of conditions" looks like a list of requirements.</p>

<p>The fix is to stop treating the list as a conjunction and write one expression:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight yaml"><code><span class="na">matchExpressions</span><span class="pi">:</span>
<span class="pi">-</span> <span class="pi">&gt;-</span>
  <span class="s">has(jwt.country) &amp;&amp; !(jwt.country in ['CU', 'IR', 'KP', 'SY'])</span>
  <span class="s">&amp;&amp; json(request.body).model in ['claude-sonnet-4-6', 'claude-haiku-4-5']</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Same two conditions, one entry, joined with <code>&amp;&amp;</code>. Now the table comes out right:</p>

<div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Caller</th>
<th>Model</th>
<th>Result</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>maria (US)</td>
<td>approved</td>
<td>200</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>pat (IR)</td>
<td>approved</td>
<td><strong>403</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>maria (US)</td>
<td>not approved</td>
<td><strong>403</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>no JWT</td>
<td>approved</td>
<td>401</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>

<p>What makes this one worth writing down is the direction of the failure. A policy with one entry per rule is the natural way to write it, it looks correct in review, the resource reports healthy, and it permits traffic. Nothing surfaces until someone audits denials that never happened.</p>

<p>If your allowlist is per-credential rather than per-claim, there is a second place to put it: agentgateway v1.5.0 added an <code>allowedModels</code> list directly on the API key, which I covered in <a href="https://webofmike.com/agentgateway-per-key-llm-budgets/" rel="noopener noreferrer">per-key LLM budgets that return 429</a>. The CEL route is the one to use when the decision depends on something in the token rather than on which key was presented.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Failure two: llm.requestModel is empty when authorization runs
</h2>

<p>Fixing the first bug, I reached for what looked like the correct variable. agentgateway exposes an <code>llm</code> context with the model, the provider, token counts, and realized cost. Reading the model from there is cleaner than parsing the body:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight yaml"><code><span class="na">matchExpressions</span><span class="pi">:</span>
<span class="pi">-</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="s">llm.requestModel</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">in</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">['claude-sonnet-4-6',</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">'claude-haiku-4-5']"</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Every request now returned 403. Not just the ones naming an unapproved model. All of them, including a request for a model literally present in that list.</p>

<p><code>llm.requestModel</code> exists, and it is documented. It belongs to the backend AI phase, which runs after routing has selected a backend. A <code>traffic.authorization</code> policy runs earlier, at the route level. At that point the <code>llm</code> context has not been populated, the expression cannot evaluate true, and a policy whose action is <code>Allow</code> denies everything.</p>

<p>This one fails closed, which is the safer direction, but it is confusing in a specific way: the policy looks like it is working. Requests for unapproved models get 403, exactly as designed. You only catch it if your test set includes a request that is supposed to succeed.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Isolating which variables actually resolve
</h2>

<p>When a CEL expression silently never matches, the fastest way to find out why is to hold the request constant and vary only the expression. I patched one field on the live policy and re-ran the same two requests each time, one naming an approved model and one naming an unapproved model:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>kubectl patch eagpol cel-probe <span class="nt">-n</span> agentgateway-system <span class="nt">--type</span><span class="o">=</span>json <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-p</span> <span class="s2">"[{</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">op</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">:</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">replace</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">,</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">path</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">:</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">/spec/traffic/authorization/policy/matchExpressions</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">,</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">value</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">:[</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="nv">$EXPR</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">]}]"</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Expression under test</th>
<th>approved model</th>
<th>unapproved model</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>true</code></td>
<td>200</td>
<td>200</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>'admins' in jwt.Groups</code></td>
<td>200</td>
<td>200</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>jwt.preferred_username == 'demo'</code></td>
<td>200</td>
<td>200</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>has(llm.requestModel)</code></td>
<td><strong>403</strong></td>
<td><strong>403</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>llm.requestModel in [...]</code></td>
<td><strong>403</strong></td>
<td><strong>403</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>json(request.body).model in [...]</code></td>
<td>200</td>
<td><strong>403</strong></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>

<p>The first three lines prove the policy is attached and that JWT claims resolve fine at this phase. Line four is the diagnosis: <code>has(llm.requestModel)</code> is false, so the variable is not merely holding an unexpected value, it is absent. The last line is the working form.</p>

<p><code>has()</code> is the probe worth remembering. It separates "this variable holds something I did not expect" from "this variable does not exist here", and those have completely different fixes.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  The policy that works
</h2>

<p>Both findings in one resource:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight yaml"><code><span class="na">apiVersion</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">enterpriseagentgateway.solo.io/v1alpha1</span>
<span class="na">kind</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">EnterpriseAgentgatewayPolicy</span>
<span class="na">metadata</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="na">name</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">governed-llm-access</span>
  <span class="na">namespace</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">agentgateway-system</span>
<span class="na">spec</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="na">targetRefs</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="na">group</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">gateway.networking.k8s.io</span>
    <span class="na">kind</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">HTTPRoute</span>
    <span class="na">name</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">governed-llm</span>
  <span class="na">traffic</span><span class="pi">:</span>
    <span class="na">authorization</span><span class="pi">:</span>
      <span class="na">action</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">Allow</span>
      <span class="na">policy</span><span class="pi">:</span>
        <span class="na">matchExpressions</span><span class="pi">:</span>
        <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="pi">&gt;-</span>
          <span class="s">has(jwt.country) &amp;&amp; !(jwt.country in ['CU', 'IR', 'KP', 'SY'])</span>
          <span class="s">&amp;&amp; json(request.body).model in ['claude-sonnet-4-6', 'claude-haiku-4-5', 'acme-standard', 'acme-premium']</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p><code>acme-standard</code> and <code>acme-premium</code> are virtual model names, mapped to real models by a separate <code>modelAliases</code> policy on the backend. Callers ask for a tier, the platform team decides what that tier means today, and the allowlist keeps naming the same two strings when the underlying model changes.</p>

<p>A denied request gets HTTP 403 with the body <code>authorization failed</code>, and the caller never reaches the provider. That is the part that matters for a jurisdiction rule: nothing was sent upstream, so there is nothing exported, nothing logged on the provider side, and nothing billed.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Why these two belong in the same post
</h2>

<p>They are the same class of bug seen from both sides. In each case the policy compiles, the controller reports it healthy, and the resource status says <code>Accepted</code> and <code>Attached</code>. The only signal is the HTTP status of a request you have to think to send.</p>

<p>That suggests a test set rather than a review habit. For any allow-style authorization policy, send four requests: one that should pass, one that fails each condition independently, and one with no credential at all. The OR bug is invisible unless you send a request that violates exactly one condition. The phase bug is invisible unless you send one that violates none.<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code><span class="c"># should pass</span>
curl <span class="nt">-s</span> <span class="nt">-o</span> /dev/null <span class="nt">-w</span> <span class="s1">'%{http_code}\n'</span> localhost:8081/governed-llm/v1/chat/completions <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-H</span> <span class="s2">"Authorization: Bearer </span><span class="nv">$MARIA</span><span class="s2">"</span> <span class="nt">-H</span> <span class="s1">'content-type: application/json'</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-d</span> <span class="s1">'{"model":"acme-standard","max_tokens":8,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say OK."}]}'</span>

<span class="c"># violates the country rule only</span>
curl <span class="nt">-s</span> <span class="nt">-o</span> /dev/null <span class="nt">-w</span> <span class="s1">'%{http_code}\n'</span> localhost:8081/governed-llm/v1/chat/completions <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-H</span> <span class="s2">"Authorization: Bearer </span><span class="nv">$PAT</span><span class="s2">"</span> <span class="nt">-H</span> <span class="s1">'content-type: application/json'</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-d</span> <span class="s1">'{"model":"acme-standard","max_tokens":8,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say OK."}]}'</span>

<span class="c"># violates the model rule only</span>
curl <span class="nt">-s</span> <span class="nt">-o</span> /dev/null <span class="nt">-w</span> <span class="s1">'%{http_code}\n'</span> localhost:8081/governed-llm/v1/chat/completions <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-H</span> <span class="s2">"Authorization: Bearer </span><span class="nv">$MARIA</span><span class="s2">"</span> <span class="nt">-H</span> <span class="s1">'content-type: application/json'</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-d</span> <span class="s1">'{"model":"claude-opus-4-1","max_tokens":8,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say OK."}]}'</span>

<span class="c"># no credential</span>
curl <span class="nt">-s</span> <span class="nt">-o</span> /dev/null <span class="nt">-w</span> <span class="s1">'%{http_code}\n'</span> localhost:8081/governed-llm/v1/chat/completions <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-H</span> <span class="s1">'content-type: application/json'</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-d</span> <span class="s1">'{"model":"acme-standard","max_tokens":8,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say OK."}]}'</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Expected: <code>200</code>, <code>403</code>, <code>403</code>, <code>401</code>. Anything else and one of the two bugs above is in your policy.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Running it
</h2>

<p>The demo lives in <a href="https://github.com/themsquared/agentic-demo" rel="noopener noreferrer">themsquared/agentic-demo</a>. It needs a Solo Enterprise license, since <code>EnterpriseAgentgatewayPolicy</code> is an enterprise CRD.<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>./setup.sh              <span class="c"># k3d cluster, mesh, gateway, agents (~15 min)</span>
./port-forward.sh
./governance-demo.sh <span class="nt">--check</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p><code>--check</code> runs the whole governance walkthrough non-interactively and asserts 24 outcomes, including the four status codes above. The authorization act is <code>--act 2</code> if you only want that part.</p>

<p>The policy discussed here is <a href="https://github.com/themsquared/agentic-demo/blob/main/manifests/governance/02-ofac-model-allowlist.yaml" rel="noopener noreferrer"><code>02-ofac-model-allowlist.yaml</code></a>, and both gotchas are written into the file's header comment so the next person to edit it does not re-derive them.</p>

<p>Next on this route: the same request body, read by a web application firewall instead of a policy engine, so the prompt itself gets inspected rather than just the claims around it.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Frequently asked questions
</h2>

<p><strong>Are agentgateway matchExpressions AND'ed or OR'ed together?</strong></p>

<p>They are OR'ed. A request is allowed when any single expression in the list evaluates true, so writing two entries produces a policy that permits a request satisfying either one. To require several conditions at once, join them with &amp;&amp; inside one expression. The failure is silent: both forms report Accepted and Attached in the policy status, and only a request that should have been denied reveals the difference.</p>

<p><strong>Why does my agentgateway CEL policy return 403 for every request?</strong></p>

<p>Most often because the expression references a variable that is not populated in the phase where the policy runs. Under traffic.authorization the llm.* variables are empty, so llm.requestModel resolves to nothing and the expression is never true, denying every request including valid ones. Read the model from json(request.body).model instead, which is available at that phase.</p>

<p><strong>How do I check which LLM model a caller requested in a CEL policy?</strong></p>

<p>At the traffic authorization phase, parse the request body: json(request.body).model. The llm.requestModel variable exists but belongs to the backend AI phase, which runs after routing, so it is unavailable to a route-level authorization policy. Verified on Solo Enterprise for agentgateway v2026.8.2 by testing both forms against the same route.</p>

      <title>Daily Cybersecurity Intelligence - September 18, 2026</title>
      <dc:creator>NetSecOpsIO</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 15:44:23 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/netsecops_io/daily-cybersecurity-intelligence-september-18-2026-4b28</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/netsecops_io/daily-cybersecurity-intelligence-september-18-2026-4b28</guid>
      <description><p><em>Daily cybersecurity intelligence digest from <a href="https://cyber.netsecops.io" rel="noopener noreferrer">CyberNetSec.io</a></em> - September 18, 2026</p>




<p>📊 <strong>9 threat intelligence reports</strong> covering vulnerabilities, exploits, threat actors, and security advisories.</p>




<h2>
  
  
  1. Cisco Patches Critical ISE Zero-Day Flaw (CVE-2026-76460)
</h2>

<p>Cisco has released an emergency patch for a critical authentication bypass vulnerability, CVE-2026-76460, in its Identity Services Engine (ISE). The flaw, which has a maximum CVSS score of 10.0, is being actively exploited in the wild. A successful exploit allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to bypass authentication on a vulnerable API endpoint and gain full administrative control of the device, including the ability to execute commands as root. CISA has added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, mandating federal agencies to patch immediately. There are no workarounds, and Cisco urges all customers to apply the updates without delay.</p>

<p><strong><a href="https://cyber.netsecops.io/articles/cisco-patches-actively-exploited-ise-zero-day-vulnerability-cve-2026-76460/" rel="noopener noreferrer">📖 Read full report →</a></strong></p>




<h2>
  
  
  2. Check Point Patches Critical RCE Flaw (CVE-2026-91843)
</h2>

<p>Check Point has addressed a critical remote code execution vulnerability, CVE-2026-91843, affecting its Security Management and Log Server products. The flaw, rated 9.8 on the CVSS scale, is a pre-authentication stack-based buffer overflow that can be triggered by a login request with a long username. A successful exploit allows an unauthenticated, remote attacker to execute code with root privileges. Check Point has released a fix via its LivePatch service and advises administrators to restrict access to the management interface as a mitigation.</p>

<p><strong><a href="https://cyber.netsecops.io/articles/check-point-patches-critical-rce-flaw-cve-2026-91843-in-management-servers/" rel="noopener noreferrer">📖 Read full report →</a></strong></p>




<h2>
  
  
  3. Gyazo Data Breach Exposes 23.6M User Records
</h2>

<p>Image-sharing service Gyazo has suffered a major data breach, exposing the records of 23.62 million users and metadata for 490 million images. The breach, which occurred on September 11, 2026, was caused by a vulnerability on an image upload server. Exposed data includes usernames, email addresses, hashed passwords, and social media integration tokens. The leaked image metadata could allow unauthorized access to private images. Gyazo parent company Helpfeel is urging all users to change their passwords immediately.</p>

<p><strong><a href="https://cyber.netsecops.io/articles/gyazo-data-breach-exposes-23-million-user-records-and-image-metadata/" rel="noopener noreferrer">📖 Read full report →</a></strong></p>




<h2>
  
  
  4. Settra Ransomware Targets Retail and Manufacturing
</h2>

<p>A new ransomware variant named Settra is actively targeting retail and manufacturing organizations. According to research from Huntress, the group, first seen in June 2026, uses consistent post-exploitation tactics. These include deploying the open-source RMM tool MeshAgent for persistence, clearing Windows Event Logs to cover their tracks, and disabling the Windows Recovery Environment. In a recent attack, the group also used a 'Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver' (BYOVD) technique involving a legitimate Gigabyte driver to disable security software.</p>

<p><strong><a href="https://cyber.netsecops.io/articles/settra-ransomware-targets-retail-and-manufacturing-with-rmm-tools/" rel="noopener noreferrer">📖 Read full report →</a></strong></p>




<h2>
  
  
  5. Manufacturing Top Ransomware Target as Attacks Surge
</h2>

<p>For the fifth consecutive year, the manufacturing sector is the top target for ransomware, according to a report from Black Kite. Attacks on manufacturers surged by nearly 40% in the first seven months of 2026, with over 1,183 victims already identified. The report highlights a strategic shift by attackers towards mid-market companies with revenues between $10-100 million, creating significant supply chain risk. Geographically, attacks on European firms have soared by 85%, while new ransomware groups like 'The Gentlemen' are responsible for a large portion of the incidents.</p>

<p><strong><a href="https://cyber.netsecops.io/articles/manufacturing-sector-remains-top-ransomware-target-in-2026/" rel="noopener noreferrer">📖 Read full report →</a></strong></p>




<h2>
  
  
  6. Spain Reports First Data Breach by AI Agent
</h2>

<p>Spain's Data Protection Agency (AEPD) has received its first-ever data breach notification attributed to an autonomous AI agent. An unnamed organization reported that an attacker used an agent, built on a well-known large language model, to independently scan for vulnerabilities, use discovered credentials to log in, and then exploit a flaw to access and modify personal data and corporate invoices. The incident marks a shift from theoretical to real-world attacks by agentic AI, highlighting the 'speed gap' where automated attacks can outpace human defenses.</p>

<p><strong><a href="https://cyber.netsecops.io/articles/spain-reports-first-data-breach-by-autonomous-ai-agent/" rel="noopener noreferrer">📖 Read full report →</a></strong></p>




<h2>
  
  
  7. DCSA Report: Foreign Spies Target US Defense Industry
</h2>

<p>A new report from the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) details how foreign intelligence entities (FIEs) are targeting the U.S. defense industrial base. The FY 2025 report found that 'exploitation of experts' was the most common tactic, with email being the top vector for initial contact. Adversaries from the East Asia and Pacific region were responsible for 48% of all reported incidents, using lures like paid consultations and fake job offers to gain access to sensitive U.S. technology and information.</p>

<p><strong><a href="https://cyber.netsecops.io/articles/dcsa-report-foreign-spies-target-us-defense-industry-via-experts-and-email/" rel="noopener noreferrer">📖 Read full report →</a></strong></p>




<h2>
  
  
  8. Malicious Calendar Invite (ICS Phishing) Attacks Surge
</h2>

<p>Security firm Sublime has reported a staggering 33,000% increase in malicious calendar invite attacks, also known as 'ICS phishing,' between May and September 2026. Attackers are abusing .ics calendar files sent from legitimate services like Gmail to bypass email security filters. These invites, which are often automatically added to a user's calendar, contain malicious links that trick victims into downloading RMM tools like ScreenConnect, leading to device compromise, data theft, and potential ransomware deployment.</p>

<p><strong><a href="https://cyber.netsecops.io/articles/malicious-calendar-invite-phishing-attacks-surge-33000-percent/" rel="noopener noreferrer">📖 Read full report →</a></strong></p>




<h2>
  
  
  9. AWS AgentCore Harness Credential Exfiltration Risk
</h2>

<p>Unit 42 researchers have uncovered a significant security issue in the default configuration of AWS AgentCore Harness, a managed runtime for AI agents. The vulnerability allows an attacker to use prompt injection to manipulate the agent into executing arbitrary commands through its built-in 'shell' tool. This tool, enabled by default with root privileges, operates in the same memory space where credentials from AgentCore Identity are handled in plaintext. Consequently, a successful prompt injection attack can lead to the exfiltration of sensitive credentials, bypassing IAM controls and encryption-at-rest. AWS has reviewed the finding and stated that securing against this is a customer responsibility under the shared responsibility model, advising users to scope allowed tools and use egress filtering.</p>

<p><strong><a href="https://cyber.netsecops.io/articles/aws-agentcore-harness-credential-exfiltration-risk-via-prompt-injection/" rel="noopener noreferrer">📖 Read full report →</a></strong></p>

      <title>Token-2022’s New Extensions: Pausable and Permissioned Burn</title>
      <dc:creator>Suliman Mokhtar</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 15:33:11 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/sulimanmukhtar/token-2022s-new-extensions-pausable-and-permissioned-burn-38j</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/sulimanmukhtar/token-2022s-new-extensions-pausable-and-permissioned-burn-38j</guid>
      <description><p><em>Originally published on <a href="https://xroot.dev/blog/token-2022-pausable-permissioned-burn" rel="noopener noreferrer">xroot.dev</a>.</em></p>

<p>The post on <a href="https://xroot.dev/blog/solana-permissioned-tokens-token-acl" rel="noopener noreferrer">permissioned tokens</a> explained Token ACL: an allowlist that is a compliance feature when a regulated issuer runs it and a honeypot when an anonymous deployer does. The same year that program shipped, Token-2022 gained two extensions with the same double edge. <strong>Pausable</strong> lets an authority halt every transfer, mint and burn on a mint. <strong>Permissioned Burn</strong> puts a gate on who may destroy tokens.</p>

<p>Both are legitimate, both are on mainnet, and both appear in the validator's own account decoder — which is how you can tell whether the RPC you are reading even knows they exist. Here is what each one does, why regulated issuers asked for them, and the three questions that separate a compliance control from a trap.</p>




<h2>
  
  
  Pausable: One Authority Stops the Mint
</h2>

<p>The Pausable extension adds a pause authority and a paused flag to a mint. When paused, the token program rejects transfers, mints and burns on that mint. Account creation and closing still work; balances do not move.</p>

<p><strong>Why an issuer wants it:</strong> an exchange-listed stablecoin with a court order, a fund token during a redemption freeze, a security token under a trading halt. Every one of those is a legal requirement in the issuer's jurisdiction, and before the extension they were implemented with freeze authority applied account by account — slow, leaky and impossible to reverse cleanly. Pause is the same power, applied once, reversed once.</p>

<blockquote>
<p><strong>Why a buyer fears it:</strong> paused is "you cannot sell", and there is no difference at the program level between a regulated halt and a rug pull. The mechanism is identical. The difference is entirely in who holds the authority and whether that identity is accountable.</p>
</blockquote>




<h2>
  
  
  Permissioned Burn: The Gate on Destruction
</h2>

<p>Burning a token normally requires only the holder's signature. On a mint with the Permissioned Burn extension the token program rejects the standard burn instruction outright, and the extension's own burn instruction requires two signers: the holder (or their delegate) and the burn authority configured on the mint. If that authority is set to none, the program sends you back to the standard burn. Supply cannot be reduced by holders acting alone.</p>

<p><strong>Why an issuer wants it:</strong> a tokenised asset whose supply is meant to track a real-world reserve cannot let holders destroy units at will — a burned token would strand its backing. Redemptions are meant to go through the issuer, who burns against a redemption. The extension makes the token's supply an issuer-controlled number in both directions.</p>

<p><strong>Why it matters to a holder:</strong> less than Pausable. A permissioned burn does not stop you selling. It stops you burning, which most holders never do. But it is another authority on the mint, and every authority is a question.</p>




<h2>
  
  
  Your RPC May Not Be Able to See Them
</h2>

<p>The validator's account decoder is what turns a mint's raw bytes into the JSON your wallet reads. It recognises both extensions by name. But it has a rule for extensions it does not know: it emits an entry called <strong>unparseable extension</strong> rather than failing. A wallet or explorer running against an older node, or using an older client library, will show a mint with an unnamed extension and no detail.</p>

<p>That is the tell to watch for. A mint whose decoded output contains an unparseable extension has a capability newer than the software reading it. Until the reader is updated, nobody using it can say what that capability is — and "I do not know what this authority does" is not a state to buy in.</p>




<h2>
  
  
  The Three Questions That Separate Compliance From a Trap
</h2>

<p>The audit page on this site runs these for every mint it checks, and the logic is short enough to run by hand.</p>

<ul>
<li>  <strong>Who holds the authority?</strong> A pause or permissioned-burn authority held by a named issuer's known key, a multisig with published signers, or a program with published rules is a control. The same authority held by a fresh wallet with no history is a switch in an anonymous hand.</li>
<li>  <strong>Does the token have an allowlist, and is it the same operator?</strong> A regulated token almost always carries Token ACL or a transfer hook with an on-chain policy alongside the pause authority. A pausable mint with no other compliance structure, launched on a memecoin launchpad, is the pattern to walk away from.</li>
<li>  <strong>Can the authority be removed, and has the issuer said whether it will?</strong> Both extensions allow the authority to be set to none. An issuer that documents when and why it would pause, and what would make it renounce, is telling you the control is a control. Silence is an answer too.</li>
</ul>

<p>Worth knowing: the platform behind this site will build permissioned tokens for issuers and will not build pause-then-rug configurations for anyone. That line is drawn on the same three questions; it is not a matter of technology.</p>




<h2>
  
  
  For Issuers: The Honest Way to Hold These
</h2>

<p>If you are launching a token that legitimately needs a pause or a burn gate, the extensions are the right tool, and the way to avoid being mistaken for a rug is disclosure at the mint level, not in a chat pin:</p>

<ul>
<li>  Hold the authority in a multisig or a program, never a hot key.</li>
<li>  Pair it with an <a href="https://app.xroot.dev/solana/launch-permissioned-token?ref=blog" rel="noopener noreferrer">allowlist or hook that encodes the policy</a>, so the audit can see a compliance structure rather than a lone switch.</li>
<li>  Publish the conditions under which you would pause, and the conditions under which the authority is renounced.</li>
</ul>

<p>The audit reads on-chain state. Make the state tell the truth.</p>




<h2>
  
  
  Pausable and Permissioned Burn: Questions People Actually Ask
</h2>

<h3>
  
  
  What does the Token-2022 Pausable extension do?
</h3>

<p>A pause authority can halt every transfer, mint and burn on the mint at once, and unpause the same way. Balances do not move while paused; account creation and closing still work.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  What does the Permissioned Burn extension do?
</h3>

<p>It moves burning behind a mint authority. On a mint with the extension the standard burn instruction is rejected, and the extension’s own burn needs two signers: the holder (or delegate) and the mint’s burn authority. Set the authority to none and ordinary burns work again. It is used where supply must track a real-world reserve and redemptions go through the issuer.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Why does my explorer show “unparseable extension” on a Solana mint?
</h3>

<p>The node or client library reading the mint is older than the extension. The mint has a capability the reader cannot name; update the reader before trusting the display.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Is a pausable token a scam?
</h3>

<p>Not by itself. The mechanism is the same for a regulated halt and a rug. What separates them is who holds the authority, whether it sits beside an allowlist or hook that encodes a policy, and whether the issuer has said when it would pause and renounce.</p>




<h2>
  
  
  Before You Hold a Token With Either Extension
</h2>

<p>Read the mint, not the website. Both extensions appear in the decoded mint data if your reader is current; if it shows an unparseable extension, update the reader before you decide anything.</p>

<p>Then ask the three questions. A named authority with a policy is a token you may choose to hold under its rules. An anonymous authority with none is a token whose exit is not yours to control.</p>

<p>— The Mint Tells You, If You Read It —</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Every authority on a mint is a question. The audit asks all of them.
</h3>

<p>The token audit reads a mint's extensions, authorities, supply and holder concentration straight from the chain — including the extensions an out-of-date explorer can only show you as "unparseable".</p>

<p><a href="https://app.xroot.dev/token-audit?ref=blog" rel="noopener noreferrer">Audit a Token ↗</a><a href="https://app.xroot.dev/solana/launch-permissioned-token?ref=blog" rel="noopener noreferrer">Launch a permissioned token</a></p>

<p>A different pair of extensions makes a balance move with no transaction at all — <a href="https://xroot.dev/blog/token-2022-balances-change-without-transaction" rel="noopener noreferrer">interest-bearing and scaled-UI mints</a> — and they are worth reading before you price anything issued under Token-2022.</p>

<p>Decoder behaviour read from the Agave validator source at commit <code>beee69b958</code>: <code>account-decoder/src/parse_token_extension.rs</code>. The semantics of Permissioned Burn described above — the standard burn rejected, the extension's own burn requiring both the holder and the mint's burn authority, and the fall back to the standard burn when that authority is none — were read from the Token-2022 program source and checked against mainnet on 17 September 2026.</p>
